title: 10 Medicare Enrollment Mistakes to Avoid in 2027
excerpt: Learn the most common Medicare Open Enrollment mistakes for 2027 and how to avoid costly coverage gaps before the December 7 deadline.
author: David Haass
imageAlt: 10 Medicare Enrollment Mistakes to Avoid in 2027
keyTakeaways: Medicare's 2027 Open Enrollment Period runs from October 15 to December 7, and changes made then affect your coverage all of 2028.
If you take no action, you are automatically kept on your current plan under its new terms, including any premium or network changes.
Provider networks and drug formularies can change yearly, so confirm coverage directly with your doctor's office rather than relying only on online directories.
The lowest premium plan is not always the cheapest overall once deductibles, copays, and out-of-pocket maximums are factored in.
Reading your Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) letter closely each fall is the best way to catch changes before they affect your care.
seoTitle: Top 10 Medicare Enrollment Mistakes Seniors Avoid in 2027
seoDescription: Avoid common Medicare enrollment mistakes in 2027. Learn how to compare plans, check networks, and protect your coverage before December 7.

sections.text: Why Open Enrollment Mistakes Are So Easy to Make

sections.content: Medicare's 2027 Open Enrollment Period runs from October 15 to December 7, and it is your main opportunity each year to change your [Medicare Advantage](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/), Part D, or other coverage before the new plan year begins on January 1. Any change you make, or fail to make, during these seven weeks can shape your costs and access to care for the entire following year.

Comparing plan types, premiums, and [provider networks](/faqs/understanding-how-medicare-works-with-employer-health-plans/) within a tight window can feel like a lot to manage, especially when letters and plan documents arrive at the same time. The good news is that most costly mistakes come from the same handful of blind spots. Once you know what they are, you can check your own coverage against them before the deadline passes.

sections.text: Mistake #1: Assuming Your Current Plan Will Work the Same Way Next Year

sections.content: Even if you are satisfied with your current plan, it rarely stays exactly the same from one year to the next. Premiums can rise, drug formularies can change which medications are covered and at what cost, and [provider networks](/faqs/understanding-how-medicare-works-with-employer-health-plans/) can shrink or shift as contracts with doctors and hospitals are renewed or dropped.

Each fall, your plan mails an Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) letter that spells out exactly what is different for the coming year. Reading it closely, rather than setting it aside, is the only reliable way to know whether your plan still fits your situation.

sections.calloutTitle: Automatic Re-enrollment Isn't a Safety Net
sections.calloutText: If you take no action during Open Enrollment, you are typically kept on your current plan under its new terms. That means a higher premium, a changed formulary, or a narrower network carries over automatically, whether or not it still works for you.

sections.text: Mistake #2: Not Checking Whether Your Doctors and Prescriptions Are Still Covered

sections.content: Provider networks and drug formularies are two of the most common areas that change quietly between plan years. A plan that covered your cardiologist and your blood pressure medication last year is not guaranteed to cover either one next year, even if the plan name and premium look the same.

items: Confirm that your primary care doctor is still listed as in-network for the coming plan year
Verify that any specialists you see regularly, such as a cardiologist or endocrinologist, are included in the new network
Check that each of your prescriptions appears on the plan's updated drug formulary
Compare the drug tier and copay for each medication, since a drug can stay covered but move to a more expensive tier

sections.content: If you are worried about losing access to a doctor you trust, do not rely on the plan's online directory alone. Call the provider's office directly and ask which plans they currently accept, since directories are not always updated in real time.

sections.text: Mistake #3: Comparing Plans by Premium Alone

sections.content: A low monthly premium is easy to notice, which is exactly why it can be misleading. Plans with the smallest premiums often carry higher deductibles, higher copays for specialist visits, or a higher out-of-pocket maximum, so the plan that looks cheapest in October can turn out to cost more over the year.

A more accurate comparison starts with your actual expected use of care. Add up your monthly premium across 12 months, then estimate what you would pay for your typical number of doctor visits, your prescriptions at their listed copays, and any hospital stay or procedure you may reasonably expect based on your health history.

[Medicare Advantage](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/) plans and Medigap policies also structure costs in different ways. Medicare Advantage plans generally have lower premiums but use copays, coinsurance, and an annual out-of-pocket maximum, which for 2026 is capped at $9,250 for in-network services under Medicare's rules. Medigap policies tend to carry higher premiums but cover more of your out-of-pocket costs for Original Medicare services, so a premium-only comparison across these two plan types is not a fair one.

sections.text: Mistake #4: Confusing Medicare Advantage, Medigap, and Part D Rules

sections.content: Some of the most expensive mistakes come from mixing up what different plan types are allowed to do together. Medigap and [Medicare Advantage](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/) cannot be combined; if you enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan, your [[Medigap policy](/faqs/medicare-supplement-plans-and-pre-existing-conditions/)](/faqs/medicare-supplement-vs-medicare-advantage/) becomes unnecessary and typically stops paying for the gaps in Medicare Advantage cost sharing. Another common assumption is that a missed Part D enrollment has no lasting consequence, when in fact the [Part D late enrollment penalty](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/medicare-costs/avoid-penalties) is added to your premium permanently for as long as you keep Part D coverage.

Switching from a [[Medigap policy](/faqs/medicare-supplement-plans-and-pre-existing-conditions/)](/faqs/medicare-supplement-vs-medicare-advantage/) to [Medicare Advantage](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/) can also create a one-way door. If you later want to return to Medigap, insurers in most states can use medical underwriting to review your health history and may charge more or deny coverage outside of specific protected periods. Before you sign up for any plan, take time to understand these rules in plain terms rather than assuming your situation will be treated as an exception.

Before you make any switch between Medigap and [Medicare Advantage](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/), ask the specific question out loud: if I change my mind next year, can I get back to where I am now, and at what cost? Getting a clear answer to that one question avoids more regret than almost any other part of the decision.

sections.text: Mistake #5: Missing Key Deadlines and Risking Penalties

sections.content: Open Enrollment has a firm start and end date, and missing either side of that window limits your options for the rest of the year.

items: Mark October 15 as the date Open Enrollment begins and plan changes become possible
Make any plan changes before December 7, when the window closes
Confirm your new coverage takes effect on January 1

Remember that the [Medicare Advantage](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/) Open Enrollment Period, from January 1 to March 31, allows one additional switch if you enrolled in Medicare Advantage and want to change plans or return to Original Medicare

sections.content: Deadlines matter beyond just plan selection. [Late enrollment penalties for Part B](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/medicare-costs/avoid-penalties) can permanently raise your monthly premium by a percentage based on how long you went without coverage, and the Part D penalty works similarly, calculated from the national base beneficiary premium and added to your premium for as long as you have Part D.

If you are helping a parent or spouse manage their Medicare decisions, put these dates on a calendar well before October. Caregivers who wait until the final week often find themselves rushing through comparisons that deserve more time.

sections.text: Mistake #6: Making the Decision Alone Without Trusted Guidance

sections.content: Wanting to research your options on your own before talking to anyone is a reasonable instinct, and this kind of checklist is meant to support that process rather than replace it. Reading through your ANOC, checking your doctors, and estimating your costs are all steps you can take independently.

When you are ready for a second opinion, a licensed Medicare agent can review your current doctors and prescriptions against available plans at no cost to you, and answer specific questions about how a plan's rules apply to your situation. A good agent explains your options rather than pushing you toward one.

Before choosing any resource to help you, it can help to look at reviews or testimonials from other clients to get a sense of how that agent or agency actually works with people, rather than relying on marketing claims alone.

faqs.question: I want to research on my own first. Is that okay?
faqs.answer: Yes, taking time to understand your options before speaking with anyone is a reasonable first step. Use this checklist alongside your ANOC letter to review your current plan's changes, your doctors, and your prescriptions on your own timeline before reaching out for additional help.

faqs.question: Will I get a pushy sales call if I ask for help?
faqs.answer: Licensed Medicare agents are there to explain your options, not to pressure you into a decision. You control the pace of the conversation and can ask questions, pause, or come back later without obligation to enroll on the spot.

faqs.question: How do I know which sources to trust when comparing plans?
faqs.answer: Trustworthy resources use plain-language explanations, are transparent about which plans are actually available in your area, and offer verifiable client reviews. Be cautious of any source that pushes a single plan without first reviewing your doctors, prescriptions, and budget.

faqs.question: What if I choose a plan and regret it later?
faqs.answer: If you enrolled in Medicare Advantage, the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period from January 1 to March 31 lets you make one additional switch. Reviewing your coverage every year, not just once, is what keeps a small mistake from turning into a long-term problem.

sections.content: Avoiding these ten mistakes comes down to a few concrete habits: read your ANOC letter closely, verify your doctors and prescriptions directly rather than trusting a directory alone, compare total yearly costs instead of premiums alone, and act before the December 7 deadline instead of letting automatic re-enrollment decide for you.

If you want a second set of eyes on your specific situation, consider working through a plan comparison checklist or speaking with a [licensed Medicare agent](/medicare-supplement-plans/plan-g/) who can review your doctors, medications, and budget against the plans available where you live before you make a final choice.
